Independent reproduction of the same root cause with a different presentation: **reasoning-channel truncation with no tool call at all**. Your P1 finding (`length` missing from the `modelFinished` exclusion list) is the load-bearing one here, and this variant is harder to recover from than the tool-call case because there is no malformed JSON to attempt repair on.

Observed on `hf:zai-org/GLM-5.2` via an OpenAI-compatible gateway, catalog `limit.output: 65536`, so `min(65536, 32000) = 32000`.

**Occurrence 1** — turn 21 of a normal subagent run, no prior truncation in history:

```
step-start   text_len=0
reasoning    text_len=129,961
step-finish  text_len=0        (+4m06s)

tokens: input 3014, output 32000, reasoning 0, cache_read 148096
finish: "length"
```

The model entered the reasoning channel and spent the entire 32K budget there. No text part, no tool part. Because `length` is not excluded at `prompt.ts:1495`, this was classified as a normal finish, the loop exited, and the run reported success with empty output.

**Occurrence 2** — resuming that same session, 3 hours later:

```
step-start   text_len=0
reasoning    text_len=132,948
step-finish  text_len=0        (+4m19s)

tokens: input 96571, output 32000, reasoning 0
finish: "length"
```

Identical shape. Both landed on exactly 32000 output tokens — two independent 4-minute streams hitting the same round number is the constant, not the model.

**Why the resume repeated it.** In `message-v2.ts`, a stored `reasoning` part is replayed as native reasoning when the request model matches the stored model, and downgraded to plain text only when they differ:

```ts
if (part.type === "reasoning") {
  if (differentModel) {
    if (part.text.trim().length > 0)
      assistantMessage.parts.push({ type: "text", text: part.text })
    continue
  }
  assistantMessage.parts.push({ type: "reasoning", text: part.text, providerMetadata: part.metadata })
}
```

Same model on resume, so the incomplete 130KB chain was replayed verbatim, and the model continued it into another truncation. Self-perpetuating: each resume replays a longer incomplete chain. A fresh-slug re-dispatch of the same task on the same model completed normally in 274s, which isolates it to the replayed history rather than the task or the lane.

That branch is correct for Anthropic, where signed thinking blocks must round-trip intact. For a signature-less OpenAI-compatible lane there is nothing to preserve, so replaying an unbounded prior chain-of-thought buys nothing.

**Two notes that may be useful for the fix:**

- `reasoning: 0` in the token accounting while the part holds 130KB of reasoning text — this gateway books reasoning inside the ordinary output count. Any detection keyed on the reasoning counter reads zero on exactly the affected turns. `finish == "length"` is the reliable signal.
- Truncation is invisible to a parent orchestrator today: the task completes with status `ok` and empty output, indistinguishable from a subagent that simply had nothing to say.

Supports your P1 and P4. Beyond those, a reasoning-only turn that finished with `length` is not a healthy resume point at all — the stored chain is unrecoverable context regardless of how it is replayed.

I've opened #40146 for item 4 of your root-cause chain (the P1 in your checklist — `finishReason: "length"` treated as a normal completion) and a PR against it: #40142.

Separated it out because the other four items in this issue are independent of it — nothing in that fix touches `repairToolCall`, the thinking-budget coordination, the doom-loop detector, or `OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX`. Your issue stays the umbrella; this is one strand of it, small enough to review on its own.

One deviation from your P1 as written, worth flagging since it's your issue:

> P1: Auto-continue on finishReason "length" — Add "length" to the exclusion list in prompt.ts:698-699 so the session loop continues. Cap auto-continues per turn.

Unconditional auto-continue is right for your case — a truncated tool call, where the model has produced real work and needs another turn to finish emitting it. It's harmful for a case I hit from the other direction: a turn that burned its entire output budget inside the reasoning channel and emitted no text and no tool call. Continuing that replays a growing incomplete chain and truncates again at the same limit, at a full output budget per iteration.

So the PR branches on whether the truncated turn produced anything usable: continue if there are text or tool parts, surface `MessageOutputLengthError` if there aren't. Your tool-call case takes the continue path.

On the cap — `agent.steps` can't serve as one. It defaults to `Infinity`, and at the limit it only injects `MAX_STEPS_PROMPT` rather than breaking, so it's a nudge rather than a bound. The PR bounds continuation to exactly one attempt by reading the previous turn's `finish` from history the loop already reloads, which needs no new state.

Also worth noting for whoever picks up the rest of your chain: `MessageOutputLengthError` already exists in the schema, in core, and in the assistant error union, and `acp/service.ts:842` already maps it to `stopReason: "max_tokens"` — it just had no producer anywhere in `src`. The plumbing for this case was built and never connected.

@bukit-kronik that's what this does — three levels, since "stop it" turns out to mean different things depending on how stuck the subagent is:

- `task_steer` — push a correction into a running subagent; it adapts and keeps going, keeping its work.
- `task_cancel` — graceful stop: it gets the reason, wraps up, summarises partial work, then stops.
- `task_abort` — immediate hard kill, no wrap-up.

All three are parentage-checked, so an agent can only interrupt its own descendants.

The distinction that took a while to get right: `task_cancel` only lands at a turn boundary, so a subagent wedged inside a long-running tool call (a 10-minute build, say) won't stop until that tool returns. `task_abort` is the answer there — it's the difference between "stop when you can" and "stop now."

On the lead-agent-vs-user split you raise: the tools are available to whichever agent spawned the subagent, so a lead agent can stop its own children. A user-facing hard stop is a separate surface — the TUI would need to expose it — and isn't in this PR.

Running in a fork for a while now; the abort path is the one that gets used, usually on a subagent looping without progress.

I spent some time investigating this and wanted to share what I found in case it's useful.

**The project picker uses exact matching throughout the selection path** — `pathKey` `===` / `Map.get` / `findIndex(x => key(x) === active())` across `dialog-select-directory[-v2]`, `home.project.add`, `layout.projects.open`, `rootFor`, `server.projects.open`, and `use-filtered-list`. I couldn't find a name-prefix / `startsWith` collision anywhere in the picker.

**The only collision I could reproduce is shared git root commit** — i.e. when `vesper-ios` was created by copying/cloning `vesper` (so they share `.git` history). `Project.resolve` (`packages/core/src/project.ts:115`) falls back to `root(repo)` = the first root-commit hash for repos without a usable remote; two copies share that hash → same project ID → `fromDirectory` adds `vesper-ios` to `vesper`'s `sandboxes` → `rootFor(vesper-ios)` resolves to `vesper`. The name prefix is incidental — *any* copied dir collides regardless of name.

Two scenarios I tested locally (in `packages/opencode/test/project/project.test.ts`, modeled on the existing suite):
- two sibling `git init` repos with **different** initial commits (different file content) → distinct project IDs, **no collision** ✅
- `cp -R vesper vesper-ios` (shared root commit, no remote) → same project ID, `vesper-ios` folded into `vesper.sandboxes`

The shared-ID case is **already asserted as intended** by `project.test.ts:344` ("separate clones of the same repo should share project ID"), so a change that separates copies would conflict with that test and the clone-grouping design.

@Hyperion2220 — could you confirm whether `vesper-ios` was created by copying or cloning `vesper` (e.g. `cp -R`, `git clone` of a local path)? If they're genuinely distinct repos with different root commits, the above wouldn't explain it and I'd like to reproduce your exact setup.

Happy to implement whichever direction you all want here (e.g. an explicit "open as separate project" override for explicitly-chosen dirs), but that's a design call I'll defer to the maintainers.

Your diagnosis in the issue body is correct, and I've opened a PR against it: #40149.

Adding the evidence I gathered, because this has been filed four other times (#20045, #22336, #22465, #25097) and closed unfixed each time. Every one of those reported it as ergonomics — an allow rule that doesn't fire, so you get prompted. There's a second direction nobody filed.

**A deny rule doesn't fire either.** Real `Permission.evaluate` on current `dev`:

```
config { edit: { "*": "allow", "/etc/**": "deny" } }

target                                 : /etc/passwd
pattern the tool sends (path.relative) : ../../../../etc/passwd
VERDICT                                : allow      ← matched rule "*"

same target sent as "/etc/passwd":
VERDICT                                : deny
```

The deny is loaded, expanded, and sitting in the ruleset. It loses to the catch-all because it never becomes a candidate.

**The documented example doesn't work.** This is `docs/permissions.mdx` verbatim, presented as the supported way to allow reads but block edits in an external directory:

```
config: external_directory allow + edit deny on ~/projects/personal/**

edit VERDICT (documented intent: deny) : ask
external_directory VERDICT             : allow
```

The `external_directory` half works, the `edit` half doesn't, and they're written by the same operator in the same block with the same pattern.

**No relative form works portably.** Note the two relativized strings above: `../../../../etc/passwd` and `../personal/notes.md`. The `../` count depends on where the session was started, so the same rule text produces a different non-matching string per project. There's no relative spelling an operator could use instead.

**The correct model already exists in three places in-tree**, which is what makes this a bug rather than a design decision:

- `permission/index.ts:178-184` — `expand()` deliberately turns `~/...` into an absolute pattern on every rule, then that pattern is compared against a relativized target.
- `tool/external-directory.ts:30-37` — passes an absolute glob to the same `ctx.ask`. That's precisely why `external_directory` rules work while `edit` rules don't.
- `project/instance-context.ts:18` — `containsPath` already solves inside-vs-outside including the non-git `worktree === "/"` case.

**Scope correction** on my own earlier reading, since it matters for anyone auditing their config: this affects only the `edit`/`write`/`read`/`apply_patch` keys. `external_directory` and `list` match absolute paths and are fine. If you have an absolute rule that seems to work, check which key it's declared under before concluding anything — I got that wrong initially and so did two other people looking at the same evidence.

**Field data.** An independent OpenCode deployment replayed the fix against its own permission logs: 125,800 evaluated lines → 19,411 distinct (pattern, rule, verdict) triples, re-evaluated with the platform's own `Wildcard.match`. Zero regressions. 181 verdicts flipped deny→allow, all of them scratch paths the operator had already written an allow rule for.

Across two deployments, every rule found genuinely inert was an **allow** — the friction everyone has reported. The deny-direction bypass above is demonstrated from the matcher rather than from a field incident, which I'd argue makes it easier to verify, not weaker: it reproduces in about a minute.

The PR takes the smallest fix that works — one helper, five call sites, `evaluate()` and last-match-wins untouched. #22336's broader proposal (specificity ranking, glob semantics) is a real discussion but a separate one, and mixing them is part of why the earlier attempts stalled.

One more data point (Linux/Arch, opencode 1.18.8):

- `time opencode --version` → **~1.8s**. Even the version flag pays the full static-import cost (see #24868).
- TUI startup: `init` takes **~2.5s**, of which ~1.8s is fixed module loading — identical whether models.dev fetch succeeds, fails, or is disabled.
- Every startup also synchronously fetches `https://models.dev/api.json` (3.36 MB). When the network is blocked it stalls `init` for ~3s; `OPENCODE_DISABLE_MODELS_FETCH=1` removes that but only ~1s.
- Local state DB grows to **340 MB** (93k rows in the `event` table, 48k in `part`) and is opened on every startup.

So the floor is ~1.8s of pure module loading for **any** invocation. Lazy-loading the subcommand handlers (41 unconditional imports in the CLI entrypoint) or a fast-boot path like the rejected PR #39821 would be the highest-leverage fix. Happy to help test a patch.

Same bug family, plugin runtime manifestation. Adding evidence from a Windows session with opencode 1.18.11.

The plugin runtime does not just truncate PATH, it strips it entirely. Verified on this machine:
- opencode.exe's own OS environment block (read via PEB walk) contains the full `Path` variable, including `C:\Program Files\Git\cmd`.
- MCP servers spawned by opencode inherit the full `Path`.
- But an in-process plugin sees `process.env.PATH` as empty. A plugin child process spawned with `{...process.env, PATH: ortDir + process.env.PATH}` receives `PATH=ortDir` only, with no `Path` key at all. Result: git, powershell, grep are all unresolvable from within the plugin runtime.

This matches #23192 ("git-based plugins fail with No git binary found in $PATH on Windows"), which was closed as not_planned.

There is also an existing, unmerged fix: PR #23310 "fix(tui): normalize Windows PATH casing in worker env". It addresses the same PATH vs Path casing issue in sanitizedProcessEnv on the Windows worker path. Worth reviving.

Local workaround that works: patch the plugin to reconstruct PATH from the registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment + HKCU\Environment) when process.env.PATH is empty. That is a workaround, not a fix. The fix belongs in opencode's worker env construction.

Hit the same root cause via a **second Azure cap** — the per-request payload byte limit rather than the image count:

```
Request content length exceeded 32 MB limit.
```

Same classification gap you identified: it's a 400 (not 413), inner `code` is `null`, and no pattern describes a byte-size cap. Via OpenRouter it arrives double-wrapped as `code: 400` with the Azure message escaped inside `metadata.raw`, exactly as in your report.

Worth noting #14562 already fixed this *semantic* failure for the 413 spelling (`/request entity too large/i` + the `statusCode === 413` check). Azure expresses the same "payload too big" condition as a 400 with prose, so it bypasses the fix built for it. The near-miss is `/context[_ ]length[_ ]exceeded/i` — Azure says "**content** length exceeded", not "**context** length exceeded".

Confirmed both patterns are still absent from the shipped 1.18.5 binary:

```
ABSENT  : content length exceeded
ABSENT  : maximum number of images
PRESENT : request entity too large
PRESENT : prompt is too long
```

#40167 adds `/content length exceeded/i` alongside your suggested `/maximum number of images/i`, with tests for the bare, status-prefixed, and OpenRouter-wrapped forms of both. Verified they don't regress the throttling exclusions from #39623.

For anyone stuck right now: the session is unrecoverable in-product, but you can strip the base64 from old `read` parts directly in `opencode.db` (`state.attachments[].url`; `state.output` is only `"Image read successfully"`, so no conversation history is lost). That took mine from 76.7 MB to 8.08 MB and it resumed normally. Mine held **48 images** — two shy of also tripping the 50-image cap in this issue.

For anyone landing here from a search: this is fixed for the **413 `Request Entity Too Large`** spelling, but Azure OpenAI returns the same semantic failure as a **400 with a prose message**, which still slips past classification:

```
Request content length exceeded 32 MB limit.
Exceeded maximum number of images (50) allowed in the request.
```

So the session-wedging behaviour described here still reproduces on 1.18.5 via Azure — media-strip compaction never triggers, and `/compact` fails identically. Tracked in #39677, fix in #40167.
